chapter: Long Island years and Battle's estate
title: No money from the million-selling Part Two Topsy
summary: Durham says he never got paid on the Topsy hit because of a publisher mix-up with Love Records and Cliff Records.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Yeah, well, the publishers make money. See, I didn't get a nickel of that million dollar sell on "Part Two -- Topsy."

Well, publisher. Battles with the publisher. He told me that Love Records had that and they went bankrupt. I just found out two years ago that that was all Cliff Records, because Phil ________ told me. He say,
Supposed to be number one book. You know, never know the difference. They (inaudible).

But then if you look at them like, for the six months ended now, six months from now, and -- I mean, those figures jump about so much and I can't see what the reason for it is, because suddenly -- well, I know one thing, though. One of those rock and roll groups did record "Stormy Monday" and he and Billy Eckstine got a hell of a lot of money for that.
Yeah, but it's nothing to do with their records. It was with -- you know, one of the rock groups did it. So that, anyway, this is what you were doing for quite a long time.
Yeah, well, the publishers make money. See, I didn't get a nickel of that million dollar sell on "Part Two -- Topsy."

Well, publisher. Battles with the publisher. He told me that Love Records had that and they went bankrupt. I just found out two years ago that that was all Cliff Records, because Phil ________ told me. He say,

"I spin the record." And sure enough, I went back and I found out it was on Cliff Record, different record altogether. But I knew Love Record had went bankrupt and he told me he had the same number. So he was honest with me there, you see.
I told his family about it. (Inaudible) well, you know --
